Four connected commercial functions. One operating point of view.

Distribute through whoever already holds the customer

Distribution · Fintech

In short: fintech cannot buy its way to customers. Trust moves through partners, practitioners, comparison sites and your own channels, and the only measures that matter are cost per funded account and retention.

Key points

  • Ad platforms treat financial products as a reviewed category, and finance cost per click is among the highest of any category.
  • Embedded distribution through partners takes months to establish but is hard to revoke once integrated.
  • Pay practitioners and comparison publishers per funded account, not per click or sign-up.
  • Give every trust question an owned, compliance-approved page that partners, practitioners and answer engines can cite.
  • Report cost per funded account and retention at 30, 90 and 365 days by channel.

Paid is a reviewed category

Ad platforms treat financial products as a category needing review. You submit licensing, business documentation, sometimes the landing pages themselves. Approval can take weeks and can be withdrawn. Certain product types are restricted outright in certain markets.

When approved, you enter an auction shared with incumbent banks, large lenders and insurers. Cost per click in finance is among the highest of any category. The incumbent next to you in the auction already has the trust you are trying to build.

So paid goes last, as in Part 8. In fintech, it goes last and small: retargeting people who already visited, and search terms that signal intent to switch. Everything else runs through the four channels below.

Partners who hold the relationship

The customer already trusts someone with their money or their work. Employers run payroll. Accounting and payroll software holds the business's books. Marketplaces hold the seller's payouts. Community organisations hold membership and trust. Each of these can carry you to the customer inside a relationship that already exists.

This is embedded distribution, and it has a specific shape. It is slow to establish. Expect months of integration work, security review, legal and compliance review on both sides. The partner's compliance team will read your claims register before their marketing team does.

It is also hard to revoke. Once a fintech is integrated into a payroll run or a marketplace payout, removing it costs the partner more than keeping it. Slow in, slow out. For a trust product, that is the trade you want.

Start with one partner who holds the segment you chose in Part 7. Build the integration properly. Reference it in the next conversation.

Practitioners who explain

Between the product and the customer there is often a person who explains money for a living. Accountants for small businesses. Personal-finance creators for consumers. Newsletter authors for a specific profession. Bookkeepers, financial coaches, small-business advisers.

These people are trusted because they are independent. Pay them as if they will stay that way. The terms that work are cost per funded account, not cost per click or per sign-up. The practitioner is paid when the customer does the thing that matters, which aligns their advice with your outcome.

Brief them from the claims register. Give them the approved answers on safety, fees, protection and what happens when something goes wrong. Their audience will ask. If the practitioner improvises, the regulator will not blame the practitioner.

Comparison and affiliate publishers

Comparison sites and affiliate publishers already rank for the question your customer is typing. They already answer it, and they already list your competitors. Not being there means the buyer sees the whole category except you.

Treat them as a channel with rules. They want accurate data on rates, fees and eligibility, kept current. They want a tracking link and a commission, which again should be per funded account. They want compliance-approved wording they can quote without their own legal review.

A listing on a comparison site is also a trust signal in its own right. The buyer reads it as "this product is established enough to be compared."

Channel What transfers the trust Time to establish How to pay
Partners who hold the relationship The partner's existing relationship Months Revenue share or per funded account
Practitioners who explain Independence and expertise Weeks Per funded account
Comparison and affiliate publishers Being listed beside incumbents Weeks Per funded account
Owned channels Your own track record Ongoing Your time

Owned channels and findable answers

Email, content and the product itself are the channels nobody can revoke. In fintech their main job is to hold the compliance-approved answers where buyers and answer engines can find them.

Every question from Part 21's table gets a page: who is behind this, who holds the money, what happens when it goes wrong, what the fees are. Written plainly, approved once, kept current. Partners link to them. Practitioners quote them. Comparison sites pull from them. Answer engines (Part 8) cite them.

The product is also a channel. A funded account that works well is the referral source every other channel is trying to imitate. Make it easy for a satisfied customer to send a friend, with approved wording and a tracked link.

Measure funded accounts, not sign-ups

Part 9 said stop reporting reach. In fintech, stop reporting sign-ups too. A sign-up that never funds is a verification cost and a data liability.

Measure cost per funded account by channel. Then measure whether the account is still funded at thirty, ninety and three hundred and sixty-five days, by channel. Practitioners and comparison sites will show you different retention than partners do. That difference tells you where to put the next quarter's effort.

The checklist

  • [ ] Paid is budgeted last, limited to retargeting and switch-intent search terms
  • [ ] One embedded partner who holds your chosen segment is in integration or live
  • [ ] Practitioner and affiliate terms are set per funded account, not per click or sign-up
  • [ ] Every practitioner and publisher brief carries the claims register answers on safety, fees and problems
  • [ ] Owned pages exist for each trust question and are the source every channel links to
  • [ ] Cost per funded account and retention at 30, 90 and 365 days are reported by channel

Common questions

What is the best way for a fintech to acquire customers?

Distribute through whoever already holds the customer: partners such as payroll, accounting software and marketplaces, practitioners who explain money, comparison and affiliate publishers, and your own channels. Paid advertising goes last and small.

Should fintech startups use paid ads?

Paid goes last and small: retargeting people who already visited and search terms that signal intent to switch. Approval can take weeks and be withdrawn, and you bid against incumbents who already have the trust you are trying to build.

How should fintechs pay affiliates and finance creators?

Pay per funded account, not per click or sign-up, so the practitioner is paid when the customer does the thing that matters. Brief them from the claims register on safety, fees and what happens when something goes wrong.

What metrics should a fintech track for acquisition?

Track cost per funded account by channel, and whether accounts are still funded at thirty, ninety and three hundred and sixty-five days. A sign-up that never funds is a verification cost and a data liability.
